source.title: The Geometry of Feelings and Nonsense in Large Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The post reports ablations of concept-vector geometry in Gemma, but does not test feature superposition, capacity pressure, SAE features, or whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions as specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The post's own ablations concern orthogonality and simplex geometry of emotion and randomly assigned word categories. Those results do not measure the claim versions' feature-superposition or polysemanticity behaviors. The animal result is attributed to the original paper and is not recorded as a result of this post.
record.test_reason: The post ablates the concept-vector geometry method of Park et al. (orthogonality of hierarchical concepts, simplices for categories) on Gemma unembeddings using emotion and random-word sets. It does not measure superposition, polysemanticity, capacity allocation, SAE features, or the dimensionality of superposed features. Its near-orthogonality argument concerns random vectors in high dimensions, not the storage of sparse features.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the orthogonality and simplex structure in Park et al.'s concept geometry appear 'practically everywhere', including for semantic opposites and random concepts. They attribute this partly to near-orthogonality of random vectors in high dimensions. They argue a transformation that makes opposites orthogonal is poor for studying or steering models, and that it is unclear how to define or identify concept vectors. In comments, the original authors dispute the joy/sadness plot and cite new shuffle baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The post applies the cited paper's codebase and representation approach to additional ChatGPT-generated emotion and random-word datasets; it does not report a reproduction of the original animal experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma's whitened unembedding space, emotion categories (including the semantic opposites joy and sadness) and random word sets appear orthogonal. The random sets also form simplices, reported from plots only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The orthogonality and simplex geometry reported for hierarchical and categorical concepts under the causal inner product may not be specific to semantic structure.

record.problems: The post gives qualitative plot descriptions without numerical measurements or uncertainty estimates. A commenter questions whether the ChatGPT-generated random words are truly random; the author agrees that the lists may reflect generation bias. The post also notes uncertainty about whether the chosen vectors uniquely represent the concepts.
record.rows_left_out: The animal hierarchy result is presented as a result from the original paper, not as a new result of this post. Comments reporting other people's experiments or results are excluded.

untested.parts: All: toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transition, regular geometry.
All: capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
All: polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
All: features spread across neurons in LLMs, or recoverable by SAEs.
All: SAE features as complete, stable, canonical units. SAEs are mentioned only as future work.
All: whether superposed features are 1-D or multi-dimensional.

record.verdict_notes: The study is about the linear representation geometry of categorical and hierarchical concepts, not superposition. The reader's T6/discusses classification and the absence of labels are correct. The comments contain rebuttal numbers from the original-paper author; these are not results of this post.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, overlap, interference, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or gives important features dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.

Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Gemma
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the geometry of joy and sadness vectors.
rows.measure: Relationship between joy and sadness vectors
rows.locator: Ablations; plot of joy and sadness in the span of sadness and all emotions
rows.note: The author questions whether joy should be so uncorrelated with sadness and argues that the semantic opposites might instead be expected to be anti-correlated; no numerical value is stated.
rows.check: Figure only. A commenter (an original-paper author) says the plot never estimated the joy vector. They report cos(sadness, joy)=0.2246 when it is estimated, so the row's reading is unreliable.

source_check.correct: Baseline: not stated. The plotted projection uses the span of sadness and all emotions. Kiho Park's comment says the joy vector was not estimated, so the projection contains no information about that vector. His separate estimates give cos(sadness, joy)=0.2246 and cos(sadness, sadness−joy)=0.6818.
source_check.locator_found: Ablations, lines 84–86; Kiho Park comment, line 150.
source_check.problem: No baseline is specified, and the comment identifies a missing joy-vector estimate in the purported joy–sadness comparison.
